content_snippet: Forward Deployed Engineers travel because the core premise of the role building and owning a system inside a customer's actual environment often can't be done remotely. Security requirements, airgapped systems, and the need to understand real workflows firsthand mean the engineer has to go to where the problem actually lives, not the other way around. That's not incidental to the job. It's baked into the name. "Forward deployed" is borrowed directly from military doctrine, where forward-deployed forces operate close to the point of action instead of from a distant base. The FDE model applies that same logic to software: instead of building in isolation and shipping to a customer, the engineer goes to the customer. This is one of the most-asked questions from engineers actually considering the role not because travel is a minor logistical detail, but because it materially shapes what day-to-day life in the job looks like. This guide covers where the requirement comes from, why it exists for genuinely practical reasons rather than tradition alone, how much travel actually looks like across different companies and industries, and how to think about whether it's a fit for you specifically. An FDE sits at exactly the point where policy has to become implementation, which means governance isn't a compliance checkbox handled elsewhere, it's a design constraint that shapes the actual system being built. An FDE learns quickly that data integration usually matters more than which model is chosen. The high-level picture is covered in how FDEs build enterprise AI platforms; this article goes one level down, into the pipeline itself. The pattern is consistent. A retrieval-based assistant gives a wrong answer. The team tweaks the prompt, then swaps the model. The problem persists, because the answer was wrong before the model ever saw it: the retrieved passage came from an outdated policy, a mangled table, or a chunk that cut a sentence in half. Practitioners who debug these failures recommend working bottom-up: check the data layer first, then retrieval, then the prompt, then generation. Most production failures trace back to the data. It is a recurring theme in why AI projects fail and how FDEs fix it. What Is an AI Data Pipeline? An AI data pipeline is the set of automated steps that collects data from source systems, converts it into clean, structured, well-labelled form, and delivers it to an AI system, such as a retrieval index, a feature store, or an agent's tools, in a way that stays current and respects access rules. AI in banking is the use of machine learning, language models and automation inside a bank's operations to detect fraud, assess risk, serve customers, review documents and support staff. It spans old and new techniques: classical models for credit scoring and anomaly detection, and newer generative AI for summarising documents, drafting responses and searching internal policies. A forward deployed engineer is an engineer who works directly inside the customer's environment to take AI from prototype to production and own the business result. In a bank, that means someone who can read a core-banking integration spec in the morning, sit with a fraud analyst after lunch, and walk a model-risk reviewer through the evidence the next day. Why Is AI Hard to Deploy in Banks? International Banker's analysis of why banks deploy AI cautiously lists regulation, explainability, the cost of mistakes, fragmented data and model drift. The same themes show up in Deloitte's 2025 EMEA Model Risk Management Survey of 87 banks and 49 insurers, where respondents cited general AI risks (46%), skills and capabilities (39%), fairness concerns (34%) and the regulatory landscape (34%) among their barriers. Those are European figures, so treat them as indicative for India rather than a local benchmark. In practice, five constraints decide most projects. Regulation. content_snippet: What Is Palantir AIP? Palantir AIP is Palantir's Artificial Intelligence Platform, a set of tools for building and running AI-powered workflows, agents and applications on top of an organisation's data and operational systems. Palantir's documentation describes it as connecting AI with an organisation's data and operations to drive automation across operational processes, for users ranging from developers to frontline staff. Two ideas matter most. First, AIP is not a model. It supports a range of large language models and lets teams choose the one that suits each use case. Second, AIP's builder tools operate on top of the Ontology , which is what separates it from a plain chatbot wrapper. The documentation also states that AIP feature availability is subject to change and may differ between customers, so treat any feature list, including this one, as a snapshot. Where AIP Fits: Foundry, Ontology and Apollo AIP is easier to understand once you see its neighbours. For the wider platform story, see our guide to what Palantir Foundry is. content_snippet: What Is Data Cleaning for AI Projects? Data cleaning for AI projects is the process of detecting and correcting errors, inconsistencies and gaps in data so that models and AI features built on it behave correctly. It covers fixing formats, standardising values, handling missing entries, removing or merging duplicates, treating outliers and correcting wrong labels. A systematic literature review by Côté and colleagues (Polytechnique Montréal), covering papers from 2016 to 2022, groups the field into six activities: feature cleaning, label cleaning, entity matching, outlier detection, imputation and holistic cleaning. That is a useful map, and the methods below follow it. Does Data Cleaning Actually Improve AI Results? Usually, but not automatically. The CleanML study (Li et al.) tested how cleaning five error types, namely missing values, outliers, duplicates, inconsistencies and mislabels, affects machine learning classification. Its findings were mixed: the impact varied by dataset and was not always positive, and it differed by error type. For example, imputing missing values usually helped, while removing duplicates more often had an insignificant or even negative effect. The practical lesson is to treat each cleaning step as a hypothesis. Clean, measure on a held-out set, and keep the change only if it helps or if it is needed for correctness.
